clue.text: Bristol supporters

parts.note: surface reading: fans of a Bristol football club, City or Rovers
setter's reading: Bristols is rhyming slang (Bristol City, titty) for breasts, so these are garments that hold them up

explanation.surface: Fans cheering on a football team from Bristol.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristols is British rhyming slang for breasts, from Bristol City; the supporters are underwear, not football fans.
explanation.definitionFit: Brassieres are underwear garments that hold up and support a woman's breasts.

clue.text: Kid and where one might sleep without a cover

indicators.note: a cover sits on top, so taking it off removes the opening letter of the word below

parts.note: a crib is a baby's cot

explanation.surface: A child sleeping on a bed with no blanket over them.
explanation.definitionFit: To kid someone is to tease them playfully, which is what ribbing a person means.

clue.text: Firefly!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: discharge a gun, the command given to a firing squad
second meaning: move very fast, dart along

explanation.walkthrough: The insect name splits into two words, each a separate meaning of the answer; the exclamation mark makes the first an order.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is both a command to discharge a weapon and a verb for moving swiftly, as in rushing past.

clue.text: A Tulsa bar needing a makeover and a fresh start

indicators.note: a makeover remodels something completely, so these letters are reorganised into new order

parts.note: taken as written
the article just before the definition joins the fodder

explanation.surface: A shabby bar in Tulsa, Oklahoma, wants refurbishing and relaunching.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' after 'and' is part of the fodder, not the definition, which is just 'fresh start'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means a scraped tablet, a blank slate, hence a beginning with nothing carried over.

clue.text: Those beaten and flipping unfit Hoskins is punching

indicators.note: a punch drives into something, so these letters are thrust inside the other word
flipping something over turns it end to end, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: inapt means unsuitable
the setter says I'M of himself

explanation.surface: A setter boasting of beating someone weak, perhaps in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoskins is' is the setter speaking of himself, so it becomes the contraction I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums are struck with sticks by the orchestra's percussionist, so they are instruments that get beaten.

clue.text: Busman annoyed with hopeless son's profanity

indicators.note: someone annoyed is stirred up and agitated, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A bus driver loses his temper at his useless son's swearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Irreverent, sacrilegious speech about sacred things is called profanity, the quality of being blasphemous.

clue.text: Spanish article about model-type with red locks

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the Spanish article wraps round what follows

parts.note: las is the feminine plural 'the' in Spanish
the Model T was Ford's famous car
Che Guevara, the revolutionary, is a byword for a red

explanation.surface: A Spanish news piece about a model with red hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red locks' looks like hair; locks is the definition and red is the revolutionary Che.
explanation.definitionFit: Latches are simple fastenings on doors and gates, a kind of lock, here used as a plural noun.

clue.text: Soldiers run at the enemy and section reloads

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
a charge is a rush at the foe
s. is the abbreviation for section

explanation.surface: An army unit storms the enemy lines while one squad reloads its guns.
explanation.definitionFit: To recharge a gun is to put in fresh ammunition, so the verb form matches reloads.

clue.text: Oh-so-clever sort of boys most rat out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters are not in their proper places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A know-all is the sort of boy who most often tells tales on others.
explanation.definitionFit: A know-it-all who shows off cleverness annoyingly is mockingly called by this informal British name.

clue.text: A black tower covered in flowers?

parts.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
to loom is to tower over

explanation.surface: A dark tower overgrown with climbing roses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tower' reads as a noun, but it is the verb to loom.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in bloom has its blossoms out, so a plant covered with open blooms is described this way.

clue.text: Car, Jaguar possibly, carrying Republican despot

parts.note: auto is short for automobile

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it within, so the big cat surrounds the abbreviation

parts.note: a jaguar is an example of a big cat
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A dictator driven about in a Jaguar car with a Republican aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Car, Jaguar' looks like the motor; here Jaguar is only an example of a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: An autocrat is a ruler holding absolute power alone, the same as a tyrant or dictator.

clue.text: Eleventh-hour talk held by most unsuitable power

indicators.note: something held by others is gripped between them, so these letters sit inside

parts.note: as in 'the last person you'd choose'
gas is idle chatter
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: Late-night negotiations conducted by the worst possible government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most unsuitable' works as in 'the last person you would pick'; P is the physics symbol for power.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something done at the very latest possible moment, just before a deadline.

clue.text: Extremely messy son dreading having to change

indicators.note: changing alters the form, so the letters are rearranged into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boy with a filthy bedroom dreads being told to tidy it and change.
explanation.walkthrough: A dog's dinner is British slang for a muddle; the definition is adjectival here, as in 'it's a dog's dinner'.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal British idiom describes something botched, chaotic and untidy, like scraps thrown together for a pet.

clue.text: Welfare state once run by him, liberal admitted

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so the letter goes into the surname

parts.note: Edward Heath was British Prime Minister from 1970 to 1974
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: The welfare state was once run by a minister who let a Liberal in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welfare state' reads as one phrase; it splits, with Welfare the definition and the rest pointing at a former PM.
explanation.definitionFit: Health means wellbeing, the condition of being well, which is one sense of welfare.

clue.text: Desolation Row will follow single by vacuous Stones

parts.note: lone means single
a line is a row

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word loses its insides and only its two ends remain

parts.note: the first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Dylan's song Desolation Row comes out after a single by a hollow-sounding Rolling Stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desolation Row' is a Bob Dylan song, but only Desolation is the definition; Row belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Desolation is the bleak feeling of being alone and abandoned, which is what loneliness means.

clue.text: Huge starter not finished in the middle

indicators.note: something not finished stops short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: epic means huge in scale
an entrée is a starter in British usage

explanation.surface: A huge first course is left half-eaten in the middle of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an entrée is a starter, not the main course as in America.
explanation.definitionFit: The epicentre is the point directly above an earthquake's focus, and more loosely the centre of anything.

clue.text: Sandy area and marshland seen around India

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a bog is marshland
India is I in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A traveller notes sand and swamps around India.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gobi is the vast desert spanning Mongolia and northern China, a huge region of sand and stone.

clue.text: Drink like Hoskins, slurping drop of tequila

indicators.note: slurping takes a liquid in, so the letter is swallowed inside

parts.note: as means like

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter
the setter refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of drinking like himself, sipping a little tequila.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like Hoskins' reads as 'as I', and the T is slurped between those two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is a sparkling white wine from Piedmont in Italy, so it is an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Declaration of occupation

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an open statement of belief
second meaning: a paid vocation such as law or medicine

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a form filled in about your job; the two halves are separate meanings joined by 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an avowal of belief or feeling and a skilled career that someone pursues.

clue.text: For Yoko, Beatles primarily must get in for free

indicators.note: getting in means going inside, so the letter is placed between the others

parts.note: pro is Latin for for, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter
Yoko Ono, John Lennon's wife

explanation.surface: Yoko Ono insists the Beatles come first and play without a fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is both the first word of wordplay and, in 'for free', part of the definition; read each once.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, short for pro bono publico, describes professional work done without charge for the public good.

clue.text: Hake ultimately rubbish European on board ship lands

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter

indicators.note: on board a vessel means inside it, so these letters go within

parts.note: SS is steamship
tat is cheap junk
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A fisherman finds his hake ends up as rubbish on a European ship.
explanation.walkthrough: SS for steamship is a crossword staple for 'ship', and 'on board' places letters inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Estates are large areas of land owned by one person or family, so they are landholdings.

clue.text: Racket English men turned round will make cash in NYC

parts.note: a din is a racket, a loud noise
E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: turning round faces the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A noisy scheme by English men abroad to make money in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' suggests a scam to make cash; it is just noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Dinero, the Spanish word for money, is common American slang, hence money in New York.

clue.text: Evil praying mantis chewed on sap briefly

indicators.note: something chewed is mangled up, so these letters are scrambled
briefly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sinister praying mantis munching plant sap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Praying mantis' looks like one creature, but praying belongs to the definition; SAP loses its P before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanism is worship of the Devil, so it amounts to offering prayers to the force of evil.

clue.text: Those one might want to punch after a crash?

definitions.text: Those one might want to punch after a crash?

parts.words: Those one might want to punch after a crash?
parts.note: surface reading: people you might hit in fury after a car accident, such as the other driver
setter's reading: punch means press on a phone keypad, dialling the emergency number of three identical digits

explanation.surface: Road rage: wanting to hit the other driver after a collision.
explanation.walkthrough: In the UK the emergency number is 999, so after a crash you punch in three of these digits.
explanation.definitionFit: The digits dialled for the British emergency services are all the same number, keyed in three times.

clue.text: 12:59 meeting?

parts.note: surface reading: an appointment booked for just before one o'clock
setter's reading: the time is spoken as a minute short of the hour, which also names a private meeting of two people

explanation.walkthrough: Read 12:59 the way a clock is spoken, one minute before the hour, and it becomes the name for a meeting of two.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-to-one is a private session between two people, such as a manager and an employee.

clue.text: Plain lover repelled half-cut Welsh rugby player?

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast, a lover of something

indicators.note: cut in half means only one half of the word is kept

parts.note: the Dragons are a Welsh rugby team

explanation.surface: A sweetheart fends off a drunk Welsh rugby player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, but here it halves the word. The Dragons are a Welsh professional rugby side.
explanation.definitionFit: Tundra is a vast flat treeless Arctic region, a plain in the geographical sense of level open land.

clue.text: Coastal inlet close to harbour and island area

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter
I is the abbreviation for island
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A bay near a harbour, an island and its surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like near, but it means the end of harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: A ria is a long narrow sea inlet formed by a drowned river valley, as in Galicia.

clue.text: Independent locals horse around with university fees

indicators.note: around suggests messing about, so the letters are moved into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written

explanation.surface: Free-spirited local residents fool about with student fees.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub; a free house is one not tied to a single brewery.
explanation.definitionFit: Pubs free to stock any brewer's beer, not owned by a brewery, are the independent kind of local.

clue.text: Sleeps around for some period of time

indicators.note: turned around means facing the opposite way, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: naps are short sleeps

explanation.surface: Someone dozes on and off for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: A span is a stretch or length of time, as in a lifespan or attention span.
